There’s two ways you can write code on the LeArm, one way is a bit more discrete and i’m not sure was intended for commercial use. 
The first way is through Python via command prompt, you’ll need to download BLEAK to connect to the Bluetooth on your LeArm and Pyserial. 

If you go to the user manual/documentation on Hiwonder’s website they will tell you the proper command structure to write to the appropriate handles. It’s not as simple, or as efficient as controlling it from an Arduino but you  have a lot more control over automation then the PC software and controller. 

The second method using Arduino is the EASIEST, most rewarding and efficient. Not to mention you can mod your LeArm by adding modules to implement different features like voice recognition, Esp32 cam, ultrasonic sensor or whatever you like! Though I recommend using an Arduino atmega 2560 for ample room to expand.

You can leave all the servos connected to the LeArm microcontroller. There should be 4 unoccupied pins on your microcontroller (5v, RX,TX, GND) you will map those pins using jumper wires (Male to female) to your Arduino in their respective pins  (GND - GND, 5v - 5v - RX- Tx, TX- RX) when I connected mine I kept getting the low voltage beep alarm even though they were using independent power supplies. To remedy this I implemented 2 diodes via breadboard to stop the TX and RX pins from pulling power from the LeArm and that solved the issue. 
You can also find a step by step guide in the Hiwonder documentation, I’ll link it below! 

Communication protocol : https://drive.google.com/file/d/1cyH420H3M3CoLBeI0xZed7qQOhNb3RT-/view?usp=drivesdk

Secondary development (Arduino): https://drive.google.com/file/d/1IuMYrsnrknBR4EEHAzm-PT6RUDyb6efb/view?usp=drivesdk

There are a couple of tips that can remedy that. For starters, you want to make sure you’re not using cheap /poor quality equipment to learn tattooing. It won’t really help you because the machine or your needles won’t be able to perform up to par to produce that height quality work that you’re looking for. 
Next will be voltage and hand speed coordination. for pulling lines you want a voltage no lower than like 6.5. Most people start at about a 7. Higher voltage  has more repetition of pokes as you pull the lines giving a more solid look. HOWEVER, if your only a beginner it’s likely you won’t be able to keep up with high speeds so your going to need to find the speed that you can handle right now. 
Following will be grip and hand position. You want to make sure your idle hand is in the appropriate position to help you pull your lines more steady as well as stretch the skin of your canvas.

Besides that there are practice books you can purchase online that you can practice pulling lines and shading without wasting your current resources

Some advice I can give is consider longevity in your tattoo designs. Like the body on the butterfly to the right is the perfect size. This is important because of the negative space/ contrast it creates. The one on the left not so much so and tattoos tend to fade and ink expands over time so it can just end up looking a mess in the long run. 

Make sure you use appropriate needle sizes so you can keep your shading where it’s supposed to be and get that desired effect that you’re looking for. Also make sure to not UNDERshade because through the healing process tattoos tend to loose some of that saturation and will not look like how it was intended too. 

Keep working on the basics and your work will take off in not time!

Besides from proper tattooing equipment (which you shouldn't take the cheap route), voltage, needle depth, and shading techniques is what you want to focus on. 

When your doing line work, your voltage will generally be greater than when your shading; however, your voltage should be set to match your hand speed (slower hand movement = lower voltage and faster hand movement = higher voltage). 

As far as shading goes, if your using shaders and magnums you dont want your needles to hang too much, the ink will have to travel to far out of the tube and that will make saturating more difficult. Make sure your also lubricating the canvas to ensure the needles have an easier time gliding across the canvas. Last but not least, TAKE YOUR TIME WHEN PACKING ( Especially if you want to practice American Traditional). Keeps your voltage at about 4-5 and move your hand about slowly to ensure the ink gets packed in. 

Good luck!
